name: Aristotelianism
scope: Aristotle's own ethics and politics (Nicomachean Ethics, Politics) as presented by the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy and Britannica's entry on Aristotelianism, together with the text of the Politics. Britannica defines Aristotelianism by Aristotle's positions: virtue as a mean, happiness as intellectual activity and virtuous exercise, and the state as a self-sufficient society needed for human happiness. The later tradition (Aquinas, Averroes, modern neo-Aristotelians) is background only; positions Aristotle held, including natural slavery and male rule, are recorded as his, though many modern Aristotelians reject them.

notes: Answers rest only on what the Politics and its scholarly accounts state. Modern policy questions (healthcare, taxation, technology and so on) are null. Strands (Thomist, neo-Aristotelian) differ on slavery, women and religion; this audit records Aristotle's own positions.

keyFigures.role: Founder of the Peripatetic school and author of the Politics and Nicomachean Ethics
keyFigures.quote: Aristotle's importance to Aristotelianism lies in his development of its key concepts and principles.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: His state depends on different roles, such as rulers, ruled and household tasks, with citizens freed for leisure and politics.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Politics III accepts birth and wealth as partial claims to office alongside virtue, so he would not abolish them outright.

abolish-income-tax.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: Aristotle treats the household and marriage as natural communities that the polis is built on.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: He treats money as a legitimate invention for exchange and rejects abolition of property, so abolishing money and wages is foreign to his thought.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: He wants moderate property but not abolition of such arrangements.

abolish-wage-labour.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

algorithmic-government.rationale: Practical wisdom is a trained judgment about particulars with no procedure, so replacing it with algorithms is contrary.

alienated-labor.rationale: Aristotle criticises unlimited wealth-getting but also treats manual labour as unfitting for citizens, so adherents would split.

all-land-state-owned.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

allow-dual-citizenship.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Politics I holds that animals exist for the sake of human use, so their suffering has no independent moral weight.

animal-use-humane.rationale: Politics 1: tame animals exist for use and food and are better off ruled by man; he gives no limit on humane grounds.

apologise-for-past-wrongs.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

arbitrator-settles-disputes.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

armed-resistance-to-occupation.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

automation-leaves-most-without-work.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Fiscal stimulus is a modern macroeconomic idea; he wrote nothing on public borrowing or demand management.

ban-cartels.rationale: Politics I treats monopoly as a clever but mercenary wealth-getting device, while he also limits unnatural acquisition, so the position is split.

ban-cattle-slaughter.rationale: Aristotle sees animals as existing for human use; no basis for a ban.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: The lawgiver preserves the constitution and he gives advice on preserving regimes, but no doctrine on banning parties.

ban-interest.rationale: Aristotle condemns lending at interest as the most unnatural way of making money, since money is meant for exchange, not breeding; he proposes no law, and the legal ban came from later scholastics.

ban-patents-on-life.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

ban-spanking.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

bound-labor.rationale: He accepts natural slavery and a laboring class without political rights, but not serfdom by that name; modern adherents reject it.

build-apartments-freely.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

capital-controls.rationale: He distrusts unlimited wealth-getting and commerce for profit but never discusses movements of capital, so adherents could go either way.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: Capitalism and imperialism are modern categories; his concern with unbounded wealth-getting gives no theory of war between powers.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Politics 7 would banish indecent speeches and pictures from the stage and rulers forbid images of unseemly actions, and Politics 8 says music shapes character and is to be regulated in education.

central-planning.rationale: He criticizes Plato's enforced unity and communal ownership as destroying the city's plurality, so a command economy would be rejected.

change-traditions-that-no-longer-suit.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

character-from-environment.rationale: Aristotle holds that virtue comes through habituation and education within the polis, and Politics Book 8 makes public education central, though he also credits nature and reason as sources of character.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Church governance is outside Aristotle; the question is for Catholic Thomism.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: Birth from citizen parents is a common definition he discusses, though he notes it is contested.

civil-disobedience-accept-penalty.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

civil-marriage.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

civilians-legitimate-targets.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Aristotle holds some are natural slaves and that rule over them benefits both; barbarians are placed among those fit to be ruled.

class-collaboration.rationale: A large middle class and mixed constitution reduce faction between rich and poor, and the state is a shared community.

class-struggle-history.rationale: He sees rich and poor as the source of faction but wants a middle class and mixed regime to prevent it, not conflict as the driver of history.

clerical-rule.rationale: The philosopher-ruler is Plato's idea; Aristotle rules by virtue and law, not clergy.

collective-bargaining.rationale: Aristotle never discusses unions and his stress on the common good could support either approach; adherents are split.

collective-defense.rationale: Treaty alliances of mutual defense are a modern device, and his writings give no verdict.

collective-farming.rationale: Politics 2 criticizes common ownership of land and holding property in common, preferring private ownership with common use of produce.

colonial-socialism-democratic-stage.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Cooperation in the polis and the good life are central; he views pleonexia as vice.

confederal-coordination.rationale: The defining sources record no position on joint councils of local assemblies.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Legitimacy turns on serving the common good and virtue rather than consent; citizens do share in rule, so adherents split.

constituent-assembly.rationale: He gives a role to the lawgiver, not a constituent assembly; unresolved.

constitution-recognises-indigenous-natio.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

constitutional-jury-trial.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Politics 1 treats the unlimited pursuit of wealth as a spurious end distinct from the natural acquisition of what the household needs.

cooperative-communities.rationale: Aristotle rejects communal property and communal households as proposed by Plato, preferring private property with shared use within the polis.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: He values a common good over class interest but did not propose state-recognized bodies; adherents like Thomist social teaching differ.

country-wealth-only-from-land.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Politics III holds that law, not the passing will of the many, should rule, and warns that unlimited popular rule becomes tyrannical.

creationism-in-schools.rationale: His own natural philosophy is teleological but non-creationist, so he would not advocate it.

criminalize-genocide-denial.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: Aristotle did not make this a legal question and later Aristotelians split, so adherents are divided.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: He ranks Greeks above barbarians and holds a universal human good, so judging cultures as only different is contrary.

death-penalty.rationale: He accepts punishment and capital offences in the polis, but never a general doctrine; Thomists accept it.

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

decide-locally.rationale: The polis is the natural community, favoring local self-government, but he did not address nation-states, and he favors lawgiver-led unity.

defeat-communism.rationale: Aristotle criticises Plato's communism but nothing in his thought addresses defeating a rival economic system; adherents would be split.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Citizens share duties to the polis; a Marxist-style stance contradicts it.

defend-planned-state.rationale: Book 2 criticises common ownership of property and Plato's state-run arrangements, so he would not prize such a state for its economic system. None of the cited sources takes up this statement, so this is a low-confidence reading of the general outlook.

delink-world-market.rationale: Aristotle prizes self-sufficiency but also trade within limits; nothing settles delinking, so this is split.

democracy-becomes-oligarchy.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

democracy-best.rationale: Politics 3 classes democracy as a perversion of constitutional government, so it is not the best form.

democracy-is-procedure.rationale: Aristotle judges regimes by whether they serve the common good, not by who selects rulers; a regime chosen by elections can be a corrupt democracy, so procedure alone is not sufficient.

democracy-needs-political-clash.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

destroy-worshipped-objects.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Laborers aren't citizens and he condemns rule for a class's advantage as a deviant constitution.

direct-action.rationale: He prefers lawful constitutional order and public deliberation, though he does not discuss direct action.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Modes of choosing kings and offices are discussed, but this modern mode is not.

direct-votes.rationale: He favors mixed constitutions in which the many judge and elect officials, with laws framed by a lawgiver, not direct votes on every law.

disparate-impact-discrimination.rationale: Aristotle's justice is distribution by merit and proportion, not equality of outcomes between groups.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Politics 1 and 2 assign rule to men and subordination to women, and Politics 2 faults Sparta for giving women public influence.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Justice is proportional to merit and contribution, not to need alone.

distribution-by-process.rationale: Aristotle's distributive justice gives shares according to merit and he wants wealth kept moderate, so he judges distribution by a pattern, not only by how it was acquired.

divinely-chosen-superior-people.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

domination-women-nature.rationale: Aristotle defends the natural rule of men over women, so he would not accept the premise that ending it is a goal.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Politics 3 treats hereditary kingship as problematic because a ruler's children may be unworthy of office, preferring rule by the best.

economic-freedom.rationale: Political life depends on virtue and moderate property, not on economic freedom; he is critical of unbounded pursuit of wealth.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: He values education and practical wisdom; anti-intellectualism is contrary.

elective-rulers.rationale: Aristotle accepts election and lot for offices and also kingship where one man excels in virtue, so the answer is split.

elite-replacement.rationale: Conspiracy claim with no place in his thought.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: He values habit, shared education and obedience, and shaping citizens to the constitution.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Permanent alliances and overseas troops are modern; his writings on defense give no direct view.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Aristotle cautions against changing laws lightly but has no theory of individual rights, so adherents are split.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Politics 1 holds that some people are slaves by nature and that the female is inferior to the male, ruled by him.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Politics 3 holds that distributive justice goes by merit, and Politics 2 criticizes schemes to equalize property.

ethnic-nation.rationale: He discusses Greeks and barbarians and a city's suitability, but the nation as ethnic unit isn't his frame.

ethnicity-statistics.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

every-country-ready-for-democracy.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

evolved-behavioural-sex-differences.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

exclude-trans-women-women-only-spaces.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

exit-over-voice.rationale: Participation in deliberation and office defines citizenship, so exit being more important than voting contradicts that.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: Fossil fuel energy policy is wholly modern and not derivable from his principles.

experts-over-public.rationale: He values practical wisdom, yet argues that the many collectively may judge better than a few experts, though not universally.

extrajudicial-killing.rationale: Aristotle holds that the state is governed by law and that justice requires rule by law rather than arbitrary will, so killing without trial is unjust.

family-wage.rationale: The defining sources record no position on wage levels.

farm-price-support.rationale: Aristotle thought farmers made a sound democratic base but never discussed price supports; no position follows firmly.

femininity-compatible-with-feminism.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

flat-income-tax.rationale: His concept of proportional justice by merit does not map to tax rates.

force-without-un.rationale: The UN Security Council is a modern institution, and his thought has no theory of authorizing force between states.

foreign-partition-plot.rationale: Aristotle discusses defence and faction but not plots by foreign powers against a country, so no answer can be drawn.

foreign-policy-non-interference.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

foreign-residents-local-vote.rationale: In Politics Book 3 a citizen is one who shares in judicial and deliberative office, and resident aliens are not citizens, so voting stays with citizens.

former-empire-equal-treatment.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

four-day-week.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

free-basic-services-for-all.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

free-public-college.rationale: Aristotle holds that education should be public and the same for all citizens, run by the state; he never mentions college tuition, so this is extended from that principle.

free-trade-promotes-peace.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: He says free people rule and are ruled in turn, which is near republican freedom, but he does not theorize it.

freedom-is-self-government-of-desire.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

gender-parity-bodies.rationale: Politics 1 and 2 hold that rule belongs to men and that the influence of women on public affairs harms the state.

gender-social-construct.rationale: Politics 1 grounds the ruling of men and the subordination of women in nature, not convention.

gendered-self-government.rationale: Aristotle holds the male rules by nature and criticises Sparta for the freedom of its women, though modern Aristotelians often reject this part.

generational-constitutional-review.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

government-encourage-intercultural-conta.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

government-nudges.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

gradual-change.rationale: Politics 2: the habit of lightly changing laws is an evil, and small advantages are not worth the loss of habitual obedience, though laws may sometimes be changed.

harassment-claims-court-access.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

harm-principle.rationale: Politics 3 and 8 give the state the aim of making citizens virtuous and shaping their character through law and education, not only preventing harm to others.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Kingship and generalship are discussed, but modern structure is not.

head-of-state-dissolves-parliament.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

hereditarian-race.rationale: He believed in natural differences between Greeks and barbarians, but the claim about races as genetic ability is not his position and is not endorsed by most modern adherents.

human-caused-global-warming.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

human-decline-since-golden-age.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

humans-entitled-to-use-animals.rationale: Politics 1: plants exist for the sake of animals and the other animals for the sake of man, for use and food.

immigration-favours-shared-culture.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: Nuclear weapons are modern and cannot be derived from his theory of defense.

indigenous-internal-justice.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

individual-rights-only.rationale: The community is prior to the individual and justice concerns shares in a common life, so his frame is not individual rights.

informal-organisation.rationale: Aristotle sees the constitution and its offices as the ordered form of political life, and treats faction as a danger.

initiating-nondefensive-force-unjustifie.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: Aristotle holds the best regime depends on a people's circumstances and character, and that different peoples suit different constitutions.

interfaith-marriage-restriction.rationale: Aristotle treats marriage as regulated by the lawgiver for the city's good, but never addresses religious difference.

intersecting-oppressions.rationale: Aristotle accepts natural hierarchy of rulers and ruled, including natural slavery and male rule, so adherents of his own view reject this.

job-guarantee.rationale: Aristotle wants citizens to have leisure for virtue but does not discuss a job guarantee.

keep-public-institutions-small.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: Mixed: the polis is the ideal unit, yet he admits larger union is conceivable; the sources do not settle it.

labour-priority-over-capital.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

land-use-tenure.rationale: Aristotle defends private property with common use and criticises Plato's common ownership.

land-value-tax.rationale: No fiscal doctrine of this kind; unresolved.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Aristotle's law rests on reason and natural ends, not scripture; Thomists add revelation to it, so adherents differ.

legal-duty-to-work.rationale: Politics 3 and 7 keep manual work from citizens of the best state, leaving them leisure for virtue and civic office.

limit-campaign-donations.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

limit-growth.rationale: The defining sources record no position on limiting economic growth for the environment.

limit-population.rationale: Politics 2: it is more necessary to limit population than property; Politics 7 also says the state's population has a limit.

local-production.rationale: Book 1 treats the household and the city as aiming at self-sufficiency, which favours local provision.

local-veto-new-housing.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: The defining sources record no position on how long immigrants must wait for citizenship.

mandatory-environmental-reporting.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

mandatory-sentences.rationale: Aristotle holds that law is general and cannot fit every case, so equity must correct it, which tells against fixed sentences over judicial judgment.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Aristotle treats unbounded exchange for profit as unnatural and subordinates wealth-getting to the good life, so he would not credit markets with allocating better than political judgment.

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: Book 8 holds that music and education shape character to suit the regime, but he treats this as good, not a critique.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: He gives weight to economic causes of faction but holds that ends, virtue and constitutions, not production alone, shape political life.

maximum-personal-income.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

means-match-ends.rationale: Virtue is formed by acting virtuously, so means shape ends; stated of individuals rather than social change.

member-state-blocks-federal-overreach.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

military-force-beyond-defence.rationale: Politics 7 would have states secure against their own enslavement, seek empire for the good of the governed, and rule those who deserve to be slaves.

military-force-for-human-rights.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

military-guardian-role.rationale: Aristotle says those with arms decide a regime's fate, but he does not give the army a guardian role over the constitution.

military-organisation-revolutionary-part.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

military-superiority.rationale: He wants adequate defense but rejects making war the aim of the state; no stance on superiority.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Politics 4 presents the polity, a fusion of oligarchy and democracy resting on the middle, as the best constitution for most states; his absolutely best regime is aristocratic or royal.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its rationale is about a monarch who rules, and the statement now asks only about a ceremonial head of state, on which the sources cited here are silent.

money-backed-by-precious-metals.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

more-religion-public.rationale: The city's gods and cult have a place in the polis, but the Politics gives religion little weight, and later Aristotelians split from Aquinas to secular neo-Aristotelians.

municipal-businesses-mixed-economy.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

mutual-intelligibility-defines-language.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

nation-first.rationale: No doctrine on nations; the polis seeks its own good life but Aristotle does not rank interests against cooperation.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: Politics VIII wants one common public education shaping all citizens alike, which leaves little room for separate institutions of a minority.

national-mission.rationale: He rejects conquest as the aim of states; spreading a form of government is not part of his thought.

national-rebirth.rationale: He favors cautious reform and moderation over radical rebirth.

native-born-offices.rationale: Citizenship in Politics III is defined by sharing in office and judgment and is tied to birth from citizens; resident aliens are excluded.

natural-rulers.rationale: Politics 1 holds that some are by nature fitted to rule and others to be ruled, and Politics 3 says men of pre-eminent virtue are a law in themselves; he also has citizens rule and be ruled in turn.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: Politics 1 explains plants and animals as existing for the sake of man, rather than as having value apart from human use.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: The Ethics treats courage in battle as a virtue and the Politics allows just war and defence, so refusing to kill even in defence is rejected.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Politics 3 denies that a state exists only for alliance and security from injustice; it exists for the good life, so a protection-only government is rejected.

no-central-bank.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Law shapes citizens' character and obedience to just law is part of virtue, though unjust law is not owed obedience.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: He wants education public and virtue-forming, but does not address religious instruction; Thomists differ.

no-transition-to-communism.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Politics II holds that property should be private but its use common, with the virtue of liberality directing the wealthy to help others.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: A king rules for the common good, above faction, as in the correct form of kingship.

office-by-exam.rationale: Aristotle favours offices going to the virtuous and capable, but through election and selection mixes, not examinations.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Offices go by merit and contribution to the good life; lottery is characteristic of democracy, which he treats as deviant.

one-party-rule.rationale: Rule by the correct constitution is by law for the common good among citizens who share office, and he does not favour a single ideological party.

one-spouse-at-a-time.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

open-borders.rationale: Citizenship is a defined body of persons sharing a constitution, so eventual open borders is a poor fit, though never addressed.

opposition-only-legal-channels.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

organic-representation.rationale: He sees the polis as composed of households, villages and classes and likes mixed regimes, but never proposes representation by corporate bodies.

parents-choose-intersex-surgery.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Law, not any person or body, should be sovereign in Politics III, and he accepts several regime types, so the answer is split.

parliamentary-road-socialism.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Citizens share in ruling and being ruled, but Aristotle limits citizenship and prefers a middle-class polity, so this is only a partial fit.

party-commands-army.rationale: Not part of his regime theory.

party-controls-media.rationale: He allows the state to control education and music, but no doctrine of a party controlling information.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: He holds male rule in the household is natural, not an unjust structure.

patriotic-education.rationale: Education should be public and fit the constitution so that citizens love their regime.

pay-for-effort.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

pay-off-national-debt.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

person-over-state.rationale: Politics I says the city is prior to the individual and the individual part exists for the whole, so Aristotle rejects the claim that the state only serves the person.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Authority rests on law, merit and virtue within a constitution, not on oaths of loyalty.

personal-possessions-private.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-12): its value rests on accepting or rejecting common ownership of production, or on private property in general, and the statement now asks only whether personal belongings should stay private where production is held in common.

physical-labour-duty.rationale: Politics 3 and 7: citizens in the best state do not do the work of artisans and husbandmen, which falls to slaves or subject peoples so that citizens have leisure.

political-borders-follow-ecosystems.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

political-decisions-consensus.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: He analyzes how deviant regimes serve rulers, but ordinary corruption claims are not his thesis.

political-violence-legitimate.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: Aristotle treats politics as the pursuit of the good life through reason and virtue, not as a battle between good and evil.

pollution-taxes.rationale: Aristotle did not address pollution; he limits wealth-getting for the good life, but nothing says whether a tax would be the tool, so this is unresolved.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: He is for the self-sufficient polis and against excessive unity.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: Politics 2 calls neglect of limiting population a never-failing cause of poverty among citizens, though he says nothing of poverty worldwide.

positive-liberty.rationale: Happiness needs external goods and leisure for virtuous activity, so freedom to act virtuously depends on material means, though he never states it as a theory of liberty.

power-shapes-accepted-knowledge.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

precautionary-principle.rationale: Practical wisdom might favour caution but there is no direct position.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: He wants education and law to shape citizens to fit their constitution and warns that changing laws weakens habit of obedience, which supports preserving a shared way of life.

price-controls-fight-inflation.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

price-stability-first.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

priority-to-poor.rationale: He wants the poor not to be so poor as to cause faction, but rank priority is not his doctrine.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Politics 4 lists the judicial power among the three parts of every constitution, held by the state's citizens and magistrates.

production-for-use.rationale: Natural acquisition is bounded by household need and exchange for profit is unnatural.

profit-exploitation.rationale: He criticizes profit-seeking exchange as unnatural but does not claim profit comes from exploiting workers.

pronatalist-incentives.rationale: Aristotle favours limits on population size and wealth, so he would not push families to have more children.

public-money-creation.rationale: Aristotle condemns lending at interest but never addresses money creation; adherents could read this either way.

public-ownership.rationale: Politics 2 argues against common ownership of property: property should be private, with use common; the same reasoning applies to common ownership of industry.

racial-franchise.rationale: Aristotle limits citizenship by birth and status and ranks Greeks above non-Greeks, but his test is citizenship, not race as such.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: No race-based legal classification in his thought; he distinguishes natural slaves by capacity, not race.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: Beneficence is a virtue, but duties are mainly within communities and friendships.

rule-by-example.rationale: He values moral education and virtuous rulers, but insists on laws and habit to restrain passions.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: He prefers farming populations as the best citizens in a democracy, and sees retail trade as unnatural; the claim is not moral rural superiority exactly.

sacred-ruler.rationale: He is hostile to claims of semi-divine kingship except where virtue is god-like; no divine descent claim.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: He advises caution in changing laws and habits that bind citizens.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: The defining sources record no position on same-sex marriage.

school-vouchers.rationale: Politics 8: education should be one and the same for all and public, not private, with each parent instructing children separately.

scripture-judged-by-women.rationale: Aristotle's Politics Book 1 holds that women are by nature ruled, so judging texts by women's full humanity is not his standard; modern Aristotelians often differ.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Self-love is acceptable when it aims at virtue but pure self-interested egoism is rejected.

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: The defining sources record no position on development aid.

separate-church-state.rationale: Aquinas-aligned Aristotelians favor cooperation of church and state, and Aristotle's polis has public cult; but there is no developed doctrine.

separated-powers.rationale: He favors mixed constitutions that blend oligarchic and democratic elements, with deliberative, executive and judicial parts, a forerunner of checks. None of the cited sources takes up this statement, so this is a low-confidence reading of the general outlook.

sex-socially-constructed.rationale: Aristotle takes male and female as natural kinds with distinct roles; he did not treat sex as constructed.

shared-human-nature.rationale: Aristotle holds that humans have a natural function and nature grounding virtue and the good life, and the neo-Aristotelian tradition builds on that; though he excludes slaves and women from full dignity, the shared nature thesis is central.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: Politics 1: the male is by nature superior and rules, the female inferior and ruled.

shut-down-tax-havens.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

simple-living.rationale: Aristotle limits wealth-getting to household need and puts virtue above wealth, though external goods and liberality also matter.

single-common-good.rationale: Politics 3: correct constitutions are those in which the one, few or many rule with a view to the common interest; the perversions rule for a private interest.

slavery-reparations.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

socialized-care.rationale: The household is a natural community that exists for daily needs, and Aristotle criticises Plato's common rearing of children as weakening affection.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: International sovereign debt is modern; he condemned interest but did not address debts between states.

spiritual-nature.rationale: The Ethics holds that the highest human good is virtuous and contemplative activity of the soul, beyond material goods, and the state should serve it.

state-finances-worker-businesses.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

state-harmful.rationale: Politics 1 holds the state exists by nature and man is by nature a political animal, so abolishing it is rejected.

state-laws-apply-online.rationale: The defining sources record no position on this statement.

strong-leader.rationale: He classes tyranny as deviant and leans toward the rule of law over rule by one person, though a uniquely virtuous ruler could justly rule.

term-limits.rationale: Aristotle holds that citizens should rule and be ruled in turn, with offices rotating, which favours limits on how long one person holds office.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Politics 7 says a state is not framed for conquest of enemies, and the legislator should aim at leisure and peace.

traditional-family.rationale: Politics 1 makes the household the first community of the state, and Politics 2 rejects Plato's community of wives and children in favour of the family.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Aristotle holds that extremes of wealth breed faction and tyranny and that a large middle class is the surest basis of a stable regime, though he doubts that equalizing property by law is enough.

widespread-small-property.rationale: His best state has citizens all owning property and a large middle class, and he opposes concentration, though he stresses moderation rather than small ownership as such.

summary: Aristotelianism, as its political side is set out in Aristotle's Politics and Ethics, holds that humans are naturally political and that the state exists for the good life, meaning virtuous activity, not mere survival or security. Regimes are judged by whether they rule for the common interest; a polity resting on the middle is the practical best, property is private with common use, unlimited wealth-getting is unnatural, and law and public education shape character. It accepts natural hierarchy of master and slave and of man over woman, which many modern Aristotelians reject.
